content: Diarrhea in children is characterized by an increase in the frequency of bowel movements or a change in stool consistency, making it more liquid than what is normal for the individual child. It can result from various causes, including infections, dietary intolerances, malnutrition, or other underlying conditions. While most cases are self-limiting, severe diarrhea can lead to dehydration, which may require medical intervention. The term diarrhea originates from the Greek word diarrhoia, meaning flowing through, and was first described by Hippocrates. Historically, it has been recognized as a symptom of numerous conditions, such as intestinal parasites, cholera, and issues related to improper food and water handling. Chronic diarrhea in children can be classified into subtypes based on its underlying mechanism: Osmotic diarrhea: Caused by unabsorbed nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract. Secretory diarrhea: Results from imbalances in ion secretion. Mixed diarrhea: Characterized by a stool osmotic gap of 50-100 mOsm. The causes of diarrhea in children can be categorized as acute or chronic: Acute causes include antibiotic use, gastroenteritis, food allergies, and food poisoning. Chronic causes include dietary factors, infections, autoimmune conditions like celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, lactose intolerance, irritable bowel syndrome, and excessive consumption of artificially sweetened beverages (e.g., sports drinks or juices). COVID-19 has also been identified as a potential cause of chronic diarrhea in some cases. Epidemiologically, diarrhea remains a significant global health concern. In 2017, it accounted for 8% of all deaths in children worldwide, with 2-3 million deaths annually, particularly in developing countries. In the United States, diarrhea is responsible for 9% of hospitalizations in children under the age of five. Children under three years of age experience an average of 1.3-2.3 episodes of diarrhea per year. Studies have shown that children under two years of age are at the highest risk, with boys being slightly more affected than girls. Autoimmune conditions, such as celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, also increase the risk. Moderate to severe diarrhea can lead to dehydration, which, if untreated, may result in complications such as seizures, dizziness, lethargy, and dry skin. However, the prognosis is generally favorable, with most cases resolving within a few days. The diagnosis of diarrhea is based on an increase in bowel movement frequency or a change in stool consistency. Severe cases may present with symptoms such as altered mental status, bileor blood-stained vomiting, cyanosis, irritability, rash, rapid breathing, high fever (≥104°F or 40°C), or low body weight in infants under six months of age. Overflow diarrhea due to chronic constipation or right lower quadrant tenderness mimicking appendicitis may also be observed. Specific causes, such as Yersinia enterocolitica infection, intussusception, or hemolytic uremic syndrome, should be considered in such cases. Laboratory evaluation may include serum bicarbonate levels to assess dehydration severity, with levels above 15 mEq/L indicating mild dehydration. Hypernatremic dehydration can be confirmed by measuring serum sodium levels. Stool microbiological tests may be performed if blood or mucus is present in the stool or if the child is immunocompromised, although these tests are not typically required for suspected viral diarrhea. Stool culture results may take 3-5 days, and some pathogens may not be detectable. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, are generally not indicated but may be used to rule out structural abnormalities of the gastrointestinal tract. Ultrasound can assess severe dehydration by evaluating the aorta-to-inferior vena cava ratio. CT scans, MRIs, and other imaging modalities are not typically useful in diagnosing diarrhea in children. In some cases, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or colonoscopy may be performed to investigate underlying causes. Treatment primarily involves rehydration to prevent dehydration, especially in infants under six months of age. Oral rehydration solutions containing an appropriate balance of water and electrolytes are recommended. Artificially sweetened drinks, such as fruit juices, should be avoided as they can exacerbate diarrhea. Medications are usually unnecessary, and normal feeding should be resumed gradually. Prevention focuses on maintaining proper hygiene and sanitary conditions. Caregivers should wash their hands frequently and encourage children to do the same, particularly after diaper changes, before and after handling food, after contact with pets, and after playing in soil or gardens.
